Part 1 · Fundamentals

What physics decides how much fuel and air H-100 needs?

Part 1 · the plan

Five relationships run the whole heater

  1. Process dutyhow much heat the feed must receive
  2. Combustion and excess airhow much fuel and air deliver that heat
  3. Heat release limited by oxygenwhy more fuel can give less heat
  4. Radiation, convection, efficiencywhere the released heat goes
  5. Natural draftwhat pulls the air in without a fan

Energy balance on the process side

Process dutystep 1 of 2

Everything starts from the heat the feed must gain between inlet and outlet.

$Q$
heat absorbed by the feed (process duty)
kW
$\dot m$
feed mass flow = volume flow × density
kg/s
$c_p$
feed heat capacity, liquid, averaged over the range
kJ/(kg·K)
$T_{in},T_{out}$
feed temperature entering / leaving the heater
°C
$$Q=\dot m\,c_p\,(T_{out}-T_{in})$$

Sensible heat only: the feed stays liquid, no phase change.

Energy balance on the process side

The H-100 design dutystep 2 of 2

From the previous slide$Q=\dot m\,c_p\,(T_{out}-T_{in})$
$\dot m = 6.8\ \mathrm{L/s}\times 0.80\ \mathrm{kg/L}=5.44\ \mathrm{kg/s}$feed volume flow times density
$Q = 5.44\times 2.5\times(350-180) = 2312\ \mathrm{kW}$E-100 delivers 180 °C; reactor needs 350 °C

0.80 kg/L and 2.5 kJ/(kg·K) are assumed feed properties for this simulator.

Combustion

Fuel and air for that dutystep 1 of 2

The feed needs 2312 kW. The fuel must supply that plus the losses.

LHV
lower heating value of fuel oil (water leaves as vapour)
42 MJ/kg
$\eta$
thermal efficiency = absorbed ÷ fuel energy fired
–
AFR$_{st}$
stoichiometric air-to-fuel mass ratio of this oil
14.4 kg/kg
$\lambda$
actual air ÷ stoichiometric air (1.10 = 10 % excess air)
–
$$\dot m_{fuel}=\frac{Q}{\eta\,\mathrm{LHV}}\qquad \dot m_{air}=\lambda\,\mathrm{AFR}_{st}\,\dot m_{fuel}$$

Combustion

Design fuel and airstep 2 of 2

Previous slide$\dot m_{fuel}=\dfrac{Q}{\eta\,\mathrm{LHV}}\qquad \dot m_{air}=\lambda\,\mathrm{AFR}_{st}\,\dot m_{fuel}$
$\dot m_{fuel}=\dfrac{2312}{0.815\times 42\,000}=0.0676\ \mathrm{kg/s}=243\ \mathrm{kg/h}$η 81.5 % at design
$\dot m_{air}=1.11\times14.4\times243=3892\ \mathrm{kg/h}$about 10 % excess air

These are the FI-001 and FIC-005 readings you will see on the DCS.

Interactive — size the firing

From feed to fuel and air

Part 1 relationships$Q=\dot m c_p\Delta T,\ \ \dot m_{fuel}=\dfrac{Q}{\eta\,\mathrm{LHV}}$
ResultValue
Duty $Q$
Fuel
Air

Feed rate and inlet temperature set the fuel; excess air multiplies the air, not the fuel — air must be moved whenever fuel moves.

Heat release

Heat is bought with oxygenstep 1 of 2

So far we assumed all fuel burns. It burns only if oxygen is there.

$Q_{rel}$
heat actually released in the firebox
kW
0.232
mass fraction of O₂ in air
–
13.1
heat released per kg O₂ consumed (hydrocarbons)
MJ/kg O₂
$$Q_{rel}=\min\!\left(\dot m_{fuel}\,\mathrm{LHV},\ 0.232\,\dot m_{air}\times 13.1\right)$$

13.1 MJ/kg O₂ is nearly the same for all hydrocarbons, so it caps release.

Heat release

When air is short, fuel is wastedstep 2 of 2

Previous slide$Q_{rel}=\min(\dot m_{fuel}\mathrm{LHV},\ 0.232\,\dot m_{air}\times13.1)$

λ > 1

All fuel burns; the fuel term is smaller and sets release.

λ < 1

Oxygen term caps release; extra fuel leaves as CO and soot.

A temperature controller that only adds fuel makes a λ < 1 heater colder.

Interactive — move the air

What λ does to O₂, CO and heat release

Dry flue gas, approximate$\mathrm{O_2}\approx 21\left(1-\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\right)$

O₂ · CO

Heat absorbed peaks just above λ = 1 and falls both ways; below 1 it drops steeply while CO climbs, so keep a margin of excess air.

Heat transfer

Radiant, convection, losses

Released heat reaches the feed in two sections; the rest is lost.

  • Radiant 56 % of fuel: flame and 990 °C gas radiate to wall tubes.
  • Convection 26 %: gas crosses tube banks and cools to 400 °C.
  • Stack 17 %, casing 2 %.

Radiant section

Radiation to the tubes

$\sigma$
Stefan–Boltzmann constant
5.67×10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴)
$\varepsilon F$
exchange factor: emissivity × geometry view
–
$A_r$
radiant tube surface area
m²
$T_g,T_t$
gas and tube surface temperatures, absolute
K
$$Q_{r}=\sigma\,\varepsilon F\,A_r\left(T_g^{4}-T_t^{4}\right)$$

Fourth power: a 10 % hotter gas radiates about 46 % more.

Interactive — heat the firebox

Radiant duty grows with $T_g^4$

Previous slide$Q_r=\sigma\varepsilon F A_r(T_g^4-T_t^4)$

Radiant duty

Gas temperature dominates; tube temperature matters little until the tubes get very hot — radiant duty follows the flame.

Convection section and efficiency

Stack temperature sets efficiency

What radiation leaves in the gas, convection recovers — down to the stack temperature.

$\dot m_{flue}$
flue gas flow = air + fuel
kg/s
$c_{p,g}$
flue gas heat capacity (≈ 1.08)
kJ/(kg·K)
$T_{st},T_a$
stack and ambient temperatures
°C
$$\eta \approx 1-\frac{\dot m_{flue}\,c_{p,g}\,(T_{st}-T_a)}{\dot m_{fuel}\,\mathrm{LHV}}-0.02$$

0.02 is the casing loss; valid while all fuel burns (λ ≥ 1).

Interactive — tune for efficiency

Excess air and stack temperature cost fuel

Previous slide$\eta\approx1-\dfrac{\dot m_{flue}c_{p,g}(T_{st}-T_a)}{\dot m_{fuel}\mathrm{LHV}}-0.02$

η · fuel

Each 100 °C of stack temperature or doubling of excess air costs several points of efficiency — low excess air and a clean convection section save fuel.

Natural draft

What pulls the air in

There is no fan. Hot, light gas in the stack does the work.

$\Delta p$
draft: suction below atmospheric
Pa (1 mmH₂O = 9.81 Pa)
$H$
height of the hot gas column
m
$\rho_a,\rho_f$
air and flue gas densities, from ideal gas $\rho=pM/RT$
kg/m³
$$\Delta p = g\,H\,(\rho_a-\rho_f)$$

Draft falls on hot days and rises when the stack is hotter.

Interactive — build the draft

Stack height and temperatures set the suction

Previous slide$\Delta p = gH(\rho_a-\rho_f)$

An 8 m column of 500 °C gas gives about 6 mmH₂O — just what the burner needs, so a hot afternoon or a colder stack is felt immediately.

Part 1 · summary

What Part 1 settled

  • Duty $Q=\dot m c_p\Delta T$ fixes fuel through η and LHV: 2312 kW → 243 kg/h.
  • Air follows fuel through λ; 10 % excess air → 3892 kg/h.
  • Release is capped by oxygen: below λ = 1 more fuel gives less heat.
  • Radiation ($T^4$) does two thirds of the work; stack temperature sets efficiency.
  • Natural draft $g H(\rho_a-\rho_f)$ pulls the air in — weather and stack temperature change it.

Part 2 · Design

How is a heater like H-100 sized?

Part 2 · the plan

From a duty to a drawing

  1. Design basis and configurationwhat must be known before sizing; why vertical cylindrical
  2. Radiant section and heat fluxtube area, tube count, tube skin temperature
  3. Convection section and efficiencyhow far to cool the flue gas
  4. Burner, draft and stackair path and stack height

Design basis

Numbers fixed before any sizing

ItemH-100 valueWhere it comes from
Feed6.8 L/s, 180 → 350 °CE-100 outlet, V-200 inlet
Absorbed duty2.31 MW$Q=\dot m c_p\Delta T$
Fuelfuel oil, LHV 42 MJ/kgsite fuel system
Efficiency target≈ 81 %stack ≈ 400 °C
Draftnaturalno blower on site

Configuration

Why a vertical cylindrical heater

  • Duty below about 20 MW: a vertical cylinder is compact and cheap.
  • One floor burner, wall tubes all round: even radiation.
  • Convection section on top, stack above: natural draft needs height anyway.

Radiant section

Average heat flux sizes the tubesstep 1 of 2

Radiation sets how much the tubes absorb; the flux sets how much area that needs.

$q''$
average radiant heat flux on outside tube area
kW/m²
$Q_r$
radiant duty (≈ 69 % of absorbed duty)
kW
$d_o,L$
tube outside diameter and heated length
m
$$A_r=\frac{Q_r}{q''}\qquad N_{tubes}=\frac{A_r}{\pi d_o L}$$

Typical liquid-heating flux: 25–40 kW/m²; higher flux means hotter tube skin.

Radiant section

H-100 radiant coilstep 2 of 2

Previous slide$A_r=Q_r/q''\qquad N_{tubes}=A_r/(\pi d_o L)$
$A_r=\dfrac{1590}{30}=53\ \mathrm{m^2}$q″ = 30 kW/m², a moderate choice
$N=\dfrac{53}{\pi\times0.114\times8}\approx 19\ \Rightarrow 20\ \text{tubes}$4-inch tubes, 8 m heated length

20 tubes at 2 diameters pitch make a circle about 1.5 m across.

Radiant section

Why flux is limited: tube skin

$T_{skin}$
outer tube metal temperature (TI-024)
°C
$h_i$
inside film coefficient of the liquid
W/(m²·K)
$R_{coke}$
fouling/coke resistance inside the tube
m²·K/W
$$T_{skin}\approx T_{fluid}+q''\frac{d_o}{d_i}\left(\frac{1}{h_i}+R_{coke}\right)$$

Coke adds resistance: skin rises while the outlet looks normal.

Interactive — choose the flux

Area, tube count and skin temperature

Previous slides$A_r=\dfrac{Q_r}{q''}$, $T_{skin}\approx T+q''\tfrac{d_o}{d_i}(\tfrac{1}{h_i}+R_{coke})$
ResultValue
Radiant area
Tubes (8 m)
Skin at outlet

High flux saves tubes but raises skin temperature — and coke raises it further at the same flux, which is why TI-024 is watched.

Convection section

How far to cool the flue gas

Gas leaves the firebox near 990 °C. The convection coil recovers heat down to the stack temperature.

NTU
number of transfer units = $UA/(\dot m c_p)_{gas}$
–
$\varepsilon$
fraction of the possible temperature drop achieved
–
$$T_{st}=T_{in}-\varepsilon\,(T_{in}-T_{feed}),\qquad \varepsilon=1-e^{-\mathrm{NTU}}$$

Stack can never fall below the feed entering at 180 °C.

Interactive — size the convection coil

More surface, cooler stack, better efficiency

Previous slide$T_{st}=T_{in}-(1-e^{-\mathrm{NTU}})(T_{in}-T_{feed})$

Stack · efficiency

Returns diminish above NTU ≈ 1.5 — the last 50 °C of stack temperature costs a lot of tube surface.

Burner, draft and stack

The air path decides the stack height

  • Burner register needs ≈ 5 mmH₂O suction at full air.
  • Firebox buoyancy plus stack must supply it, with margin for hot days.
  • A damper (HV-400) trims draft; a minimum opening avoids a closed stack.
From Part 1$\Delta p=gH(\rho_a-\rho_f)$

Safety in the design

What the design adds to protect

Tubes

Low-flow trip, skin thermocouples, high-outlet trip.

Firebox

Purge before light-off, flame scanner, explosion doors.

Fuel

Double block and bleed valves, low-pressure trip.

Part 2 · summary

What Part 2 settled

  • The design basis fixes duty, fuel and efficiency before sizing.
  • Radiant area = duty ÷ flux; flux is limited by tube skin temperature.
  • Convection surface sets stack temperature and so efficiency.
  • Natural draft sets the stack height; safety systems protect tubes, box and fuel.

Part 3 · Operation

How do you run H-100 safely and efficiently?

Part 3 · the plan

Five operating habits

  1. The operating envelopethe limits you watch every shift
  2. Startup through the BMSpurge, light at low fire, bring up
  3. Changing rate: air leads fuelwhy the order of moves matters
  4. Optimising excess airhow low O₂ can safely go
  5. Shutdown and emergenciessafe-park, trip, cool down

Operating envelope

The limits you watch

VariableNormalWhy it matters
Outlet TT-040350 ± 1 °Creactor V-200 inlet
Firebox O₂ AI-0281.5–4 %complete combustion
CO AI-026< 100 ppmno unburned fuel
Firebox PI-003negativeno flue gas leaks out
Tube skin TI-024< 430 °Ctube life

Startup through the BMS

Purge, light, bring up

BMS = burner management system: the logic that permits and supervises firing.

1

Establish feed ≥ 3.4 L/s; open air valve and damper wide.

2

Purge: ≥ 1700 kg/h air for the purge time clears any fuel vapour.

3

Light at low fire: TIC-030 manual, output 10–20 %; 10 s trial.

4

Raise air, then feed and fuel; switch TIC-030 to automatic.

Changing rate

Air leads fuel up, fuel leads air down

From Part 1$Q_{rel}=\min(\dot m_{fuel}\mathrm{LHV},\ 0.232\,\dot m_{air}\times13.1)$
  • Raising fuel first can pass λ = 1 for a moment: CO, soot, even a puff.
  • Lowering air first does the same on the way down.

In rev A nothing links air to fuel — the operator is the link.

Interactive — push the feed

What happens when air is not raised

Fuel · λ

outlet temperature TT-040 reached (set point 350 °C)

Above about 7.3 L/s with air held, the outlet falls although fuel rises — raise air first and the same feed reaches 350 °C.

Interactive — trim the air

How low can O₂ go?

Efficiency · CO

Band chosen in the OTS: 1.5–2.0 %.

Below about 1.3 % O₂ CO rises faster than efficiency improves — the optimum is a margin above the CO knee, not the minimum O₂.

Shutdown and emergencies

Make it safe first

Safe-park

TIC-030 manual, fuel to normal, feed to design; then investigate.

Normal shutdown

Lower fuel, then feed, then air; stop burner; cool with feed flowing.

Emergency

BMS trip, confirm fuel isolated, keep feed and draft air on.

Part 3 · summary

What Part 3 settled

  • Five limits: outlet, O₂, CO, firebox pressure, tube skin.
  • Startup: purge, low-fire light-off, then air ahead of fuel.
  • Air leads fuel up; fuel leads air down.
  • Optimum O₂ sits above the CO knee; safe-park before investigating.

Part 4 · Process description

Where does the feed go and what happens to it?

Part 4 · the plan

Follow four streams

  1. Feed systemtank, pumps, preheater, flow control
  2. Heater coilconvection first, then radiant, then reactor
  3. Fuel and airhow each reaches the burner
  4. Flue gasfrom flame to stack, and what is measured

Interactive — click a stream

The process at a glance

Click a coloured stream to see its design conditions.

Feed gains 140 °C in E-100 and 170 °C in H-100 — the heater only supplies what the preheater does not.

Feed system

Tank, pumps, preheater, flow control

  • P-100A pumps from TK-101 at about 1030 kPa; P-100B is the spare.
  • E-100 heats feed 40 → 180 °C with heating fluid from Unit A.
  • FIC-003 holds 6.8 L/s through FV-010, which fails open.

Heater coil

Convection first, then radiant

  • Feed enters the top convection tubes at 180 °C (TI-020).
  • It flows down, against the rising gas, to 233 °C at the crossover (TI-022).
  • Radiant wall tubes take it to 350 °C (TT-040), then to reactor V-200.

Interactive — change the feed rate

Temperatures along the path

Air raised with fuel (10 % excess held).

Fuel · stack

More feed, same outlet: the crossover drops and the firebox gets hotter — the radiant section carries the extra duty.

Fuel and air

Two routes to one burner

Fuel oil

V-121 → FI-001 → XV-301, bleed XV-303, XV-302 → FV-300 → gun at 600 kPa.

Air

F-100 screen → FV-200 → windbox, pulled by draft; 3892 kg/h.

Flue gas

From flame to stack

  • Firebox gas ≈ 990 °C (TIAH-023); O₂ 2.1 % (AI-028).
  • Convection cools it to 400 °C (TI-021).
  • Stack exit O₂ 3.2 % (AI-029) — higher, because air leaks in above the firebox.

Part 4 · summary

What Part 4 settled

  • Feed: TK-101 → P-100 → E-100 (180 °C) → FV-010 → convection → radiant → V-200 (350 °C).
  • Fuel and air meet only at the burner.
  • Flue gas leaves at 400 °C; stack O₂ reads above firebox O₂.

Fail-safe positions

What each valve does on failure

FV-010 fail open

Feed keeps flowing: the coil stays cooled.

FV-300 fail closed

Fuel stops: no uncontrolled firing.

FV-200, HV-400 fail open

Air and draft stay available to purge.

Part 5 · summary

What Part 5 settled

  • Tag letters give the measured variable and the function.
  • Three loops: FIC-003 feed, TIC-030 fuel, FIC-005 air — air is not tied to fuel in rev A.

Part 7 · The units around H-100

What do the other units in the process do?

Part 7 · the plan

Four supporting units

  1. Feed pumps P-100A/Bwhere the pressure comes from
  2. Preheater E-100how it sets the heater's duty
  3. Fuel oil trainshut-off, bleed and control
  4. Reactor V-200why it needs a steady 350 °C

Feed pumps

Pump curve meets system curve

$\Delta p_{pump}$
pressure the pump adds, falls with flow
kPa
$\Delta p_{sys}$
pressure the system needs: coil, valve, reactor
kPa
$C_v$
valve flow coefficient, grows with opening
–
$$\Delta p_{pump}=a-b\,F^2\qquad \Delta p_{sys}=p_0+\left(k+\tfrac{1}{C_v^2}\right)F^2$$

Operating flow is where the two curves cross.

Interactive — open FV-010

How the flow valve sets the operating point

Previous slide$a-bF^2=p_0+(k+C_v^{-2})F^2$

Flow · discharge

Coking steepens the system curve; FIC-003 hides it by opening FV-010 — until the valve runs out.

Preheater E-100

Every degree from E-100 is fuel saved

$\varepsilon_{E}$
E-100 effectiveness: achieved ÷ maximum temperature rise
–
$T_{hot}$
heating fluid inlet (TI-063)
230 °C
$$T_{010}=T_0+\varepsilon_E\,(T_{hot}-T_0)$$

Fouling or less heating fluid lowers $\varepsilon_E$; H-100 must fire harder.

Interactive — foul the preheater

E-100 performance shifts load to H-100

Previous slide$T_{010}=T_0+\varepsilon_E(T_{hot}-T_0)$

TI-010

H-100 duty · fuel

Losing 20 °C of preheat adds about 270 kW to H-100 — with air held, that alone can push the box toward λ = 1.

Fuel oil train

Double block and bleed

  • XV-301 and XV-302 close on any trip.
  • XV-303 between them opens: leaking fuel goes to a safe place, not the burner.
  • FV-300 then controls flow; PIAL-020 watches gun pressure.

Reactor V-200

Why the outlet must be steady

  • Reaction rate rises steeply with temperature: a few degrees change conversion.
  • Too hot: selectivity loss and faster catalyst ageing.
  • That is why TT-040 is held to ± 1 °C and TSHH-025 trips at 375 °C.

Part 7 · summary

What Part 7 settled

  • Pump and system curves set the feed; FV-010 moves the crossing.
  • E-100 preheat directly sets H-100 duty and fuel.
  • Double block and bleed isolates fuel on a trip.
  • V-200 needs a steady 350 °C.

How exercises are graded

Two kinds of score

Continuous score

Starts at 100; loses points while outlet, O₂, CO, pressure or skin are off, or alarms wait.

Exercise grades

Procedures /10, reading sheet /15, what-if, trend matching, scrambles — listed in Debrief.

Procedures

Five graded procedures

ObjectiveProcedureGraded on
Start a cold heater safely and line out at designCold startup through the BMSsteps in order, no trip, within 90 min
Take the heater down in an orderly wayNormal shutdownfuel before feed before air; cool with flow
Trip and make safe within one minuteEmergency shutdownfuel isolated in 60 s; feed and draft kept
Recover a fuel-rich heater and reach 8.2 L/sFeed-push recoverysafe-park, air first, 350 °C, λ > 1
Trim air to the lowest safe O₂ and hold it through a fuel changeOptimisation: minimum safe excess airO₂ 1.5–2.0 %, CO < 100 ppm at 25 min

The six-stage method

StageYou produce
1 Engagerun, safe-park or shut down, and why
2 Defineproblem statement, IS / IS NOT, target
3 Explorefundamentals, consistency checks, trends
4 Planhypotheses, each with a test

Instrument pairs that should agree

Pick a pair.

A fault shows where two instruments that should agree stop agreeing — that disagreement is the first clue in every troubleshooting case.

Part 8 · summary

What Part 8 settled

  • Every exercise has one objective; read it before you start.
  • Procedures train sequence; training exercises train one skill each.
  • Troubleshooting cases train the six-stage method on hidden causes.
  • Consistency checks between instruments are the first clue.

Before you open the simulator

Key Takeaways

1

Move air before fuel on the way up.

2

Watch firebox O₂ and CO, not only the outlet temperature.

3

Check two instruments before believing one.

4

Safe-park first, investigate second.
